planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep about two weeks after the last frost in full sun; this 1955 semi-cactus type opens narrow, slightly twisted peachy-pink petals atop notably dark stems.

directions: Preference is a semi-cactus dahlia introduced in 1955, opening narrow peachy-pink petals on notably dark stems that make the 3-5 inch blooms pop against the foliage. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the eye facing up once soil has warmed after the last frost. Pinch the central growing tip once the plant reaches about a foot tall to encourage bushy branching and more flowers. Stake the stems early, since the four-foot plants can topple under their own bloom load by late summer.
sources: Old House Gardens — Preference dahlia variety notes

planting.note: Set tubers 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost; drive a stake in at planting time since this is a sturdy, four- to five-foot ball dahlia.

directions: Kaiser Wilhelm is one of a small handful of dahlia cultivars documented to survive from the flood of varieties bred in the 1880s, having been introduced in 1881 and kept in continuous cultivation since. Its tightly packed ball-form flowers open a custard yellow brushed with burgundy toward the tips around a small green button eye, a color combination unlike most modern ball dahlias. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the soil has warmed, and expect sturdy four- to five-foot stems that benefit from a stake driven in at planting time. Gardeners growing it are effectively maintaining a living 19th-century horticultural antique.
sources: Old House Gardens — Kaiser Wilhelm dahlia variety notes
American Dahlia Society — dahlia flower-form classification

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep, eye facing upward, once soil has warmed after the last frost; space plants to let the bushy 3-4 foot habit fill in.

directions: Golden Torch, introduced in 1971, produces tightly quilled, sunshine-yellow ball-form blooms whose orderly ranks of petals have drawn comparisons to honeycomb. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep with the eye facing upward once soil has warmed, spacing plants to give the 3-4 foot bushy habit room to fill in. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep the compact plant producing its abundant 3-4 inch blooms through late summer. Its clean golden color and dependable bloom count make it equally useful as a cut flower and a border plant.
sources: Old House Gardens — Golden Torch dahlia variety notes
American Dahlia Society — dahlia flower-form classification

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake early, since the tall stems carry heavy waterlily-type blooms that bow in wind and rain.

directions: Winsome is an American waterlily-type dahlia introduced in 1940 and still grown today as one of the older named varieties in that flower form. Its broad, flattened petals open in rose and gold tones, producing palm-sized 4-5 inch blooms on sturdy 4-5 foot stems. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake plants early, since the tall stems carry heavy flowers that bow in wind and rain. Regular deadheading keeps this heirloom variety flowering steadily from midsummer into fall.
sources: Old House Gardens — Winsome dahlia variety notes

common_name: Stolz von Berlin Dahlia (Pride of Berlin)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in full sun after the last frost; the bushy 3-4 foot plants produce abundant small ball-form blooms that nod slightly rather than facing straight up.

directions: Stolz von Berlin, also known by its English translation Pride of Berlin, was introduced in Germany in 1884 and remains one of the oldest ball-type dahlias still commercially available. Its small, plump, soft lavender-pink ball flowers nod slightly on the stem rather than facing straight up, a trait that sets it apart from stiffer modern ball dahlias. Grow it in full sun with tubers planted 4-6 inches deep after the last frost, allowing the bushy 3-4 foot plants to produce their abundant 2-2.5 inch blooms through summer. Its long documented history makes it a favorite among growers of heirloom dahlias.
sources: Old House Gardens — Stolz von Berlin dahlia variety notes
American Dahlia Society — dahlia flower-form classification

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the danger of frost has passed, spacing plants to accommodate the compact 30-40 inch pompon habit.

directions: Bantling is a pompon dahlia introduced in 1979, its neat rows of rolled orange petals forming a tidy, lollipop-like sphere about 2 inches across. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the danger of frost has passed, spacing plants to accommodate the compact 30-40 inch habit typical of pompon-class dahlias. Because the flowers are small and borne in quantity, Bantling performs especially well as a cut flower and benefits from frequent picking to keep new buds forming. Its tidy, geometric petal arrangement makes it a favorite among growers who exhibit pompon-class dahlias.
sources: Old House Gardens — Bantling dahlia variety notes

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-5 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost; this dwarf dahlia needs only light support for its abundant pink blooms.

directions: Berliner Kleene is a dwarf dahlia introduced in 1967, standing only 15-16 inches tall yet producing surprisingly large 4-6 inch formal decorative pink blooms relative to its small stature. Its low, bushy habit suits raised beds, containers, and the front of a border where taller dahlias would overwhelm the space. Plant tubers 3-5 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost, and expect this compact variety to flower heavily through midsummer. Minimal staking is needed given its short stems, though a light support ring helps keep the abundant blooms from flopping onto the soil.
sources: Old House Gardens — Berliner Kleene dahlia variety notes
American Dahlia Society — dahlia flower-form classification

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake taller stems, since this historic pompon variety can grow surprisingly lanky in rich soil.

directions: White Aster, introduced in 1879, is often cited among heirloom dahlia growers as one of the oldest dahlia varieties still in general cultivation. Its small, ivory pompon flowers carry a honey-gold glow at the center and are borne in generous numbers on plants that range from three to five feet tall depending on growing conditions. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake the taller stems, since this historic variety can grow surprisingly lanky in rich soil. Its diminutive 1-2 inch blooms suit it better to arrangements and mixed bouquets than to use as a single dramatic specimen flower.
sources: Old House Gardens — White Aster dahlia variety notes

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake the 4-5 foot stems before the large cactus-form flowers add their weight.

directions: Nita is a variegated cactus-form sport of the earlier purplish-red cactus dahlia Juanita, introduced in 1959. Its shaggy petals are a lavender-pink streaked and stippled with burgundy, giving each 6 inch bloom a mottled, hand-painted appearance distinct from its solid-colored parent. Grow it in full sun with tubers planted 4-6 inches deep after the last frost, staking the 4-5 foot stems before the large flowers add their weight. Because sports like Nita can occasionally revert toward the coloring of their parent plant, watch for and remove any solid-colored stems so the variegated pattern is preserved.
sources: Old House Gardens — Nita dahlia variety notes

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost, giving plants extra width in the bed since this dwarf waterlily dahlia spreads almost as wide as it grows tall.

directions: Lutt Wichen is an unusually dwarf waterlily dahlia introduced in 1941, reaching only 2-3 feet tall while spreading nearly as wide, almost like a flowering groundcover. Its gardenia-like, creamy white 3 inch blooms open against deep green foliage and show well even in small gardens or containers where taller waterlily dahlias would be impractical. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost, giving plants a little extra width in the bed to accommodate their spreading habit. Light, regular deadheading keeps this compact heirloom blooming steadily through the growing season.
sources: Old House Gardens — Lutt Wichen dahlia variety notes
